summary: Extends IS-IS so any cryptographic authentication algorithm can be used, in addition to the plain-text and HMAC-MD5 schemes already defined. This lets operators choose stronger or newer algorithms, such as the SHA family, without changing the protocol again. It is on the standards track and has been updated by later documents.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5310 lets IS-IS routers authenticate routing messages with HMAC and a selected SHA-family hash. Each message carries a key identifier so the receiver can choose the matching key and algorithm.

subtitle: A flexible IS-IS authentication format that uses a key identifier and HMAC with SHA-family hash functions.

tldr.problem: IS-IS authentication was defined for cleartext passwords and HMAC-MD5, while the RFC notes concerns about the long-term strength of MD5.
tldr.mechanism: CRYPTO_AUTH adds authentication type 3 to IS-IS authentication TLV 10. A two-octet Key ID selects a security association containing the HMAC algorithm and key used to authenticate the PDU.
tldr.outcome: The format supports the SHA hash family named in the RFC but provides no confidentiality or replay protection. RFC 5310 has been updated by RFC 6232 and RFC 6233.

today: RFC 5310 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2009. It has been updated by RFC 6232 and RFC 6233.

sections.title: Why IS-IS Adds Generic Authentication
sections.content:
IS-IS carries an authentication TLV, type 10, in its protocol data units (PDUs). Earlier defined methods included cleartext passwords and HMAC-MD5. RFC 5310 adds CRYPTO_AUTH, a generic authentication type, and describes its use with HMAC and SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, or SHA-512.

The RFC also replaces per-interface keys with Key IDs that identify security associations. It says the method authenticates that a PDU came from a system with access to the area or domain password, but does not conceal the PDU contents.
sections.plainLanguage: IS-IS routers can use CRYPTO_AUTH to check whether a routing message was made with a shared secret. The method keeps the message readable and does not identify one specific router as its origin.

sections.title: The Security Association and Key ID
sections.content:
An IS-IS Security Association (SA) is a set of parameters shared by legitimate IS-IS speakers. It includes a two-octet unsigned Key ID, an authentication algorithm, and an authentication key. The network operator configures the Key ID, and a receiver uses the ID in an incoming PDU to select the matching SA.

The algorithm and key are not sent in cleartext in the PDU. A Key ID can select a different algorithm and key, so multiple active associations can support a change without disrupting an IS-IS peering. The RFC describes key-chain operation as outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The Key ID tells a router which configured algorithm and secret to use for a message. Operators can keep more than one association available while changing keys or algorithms.

sections.title: CRYPTO_AUTH in the Authentication TLV
sections.content:
Authentication type 3 marks CRYPTO_AUTH in the existing IS-IS authentication TLV, type 10. After the TLV type, length, and authentication type come the two-octet Key ID and the variable-length authentication data. The data length matches the output size of the selected hash.

The TLV length is 23 for HMAC-SHA-1, 31 for HMAC-SHA-224, 35 for HMAC-SHA-256, 51 for HMAC-SHA-384, and 67 for HMAC-SHA-512. These lengths include the authentication type and Key ID, as well as the authentication data.
sections.plainLanguage: Each authenticated PDU carries type 3, the Key ID, and the HMAC result. Hashes with larger outputs require a longer authentication field.

sections.title: How the HMAC Result Is Computed
sections.content:
The RFC follows the HMAC procedure in FIPS 198. It first prepares a key of the hash output length: a longer key is hashed, and a shorter key is padded with zeroes. It defines Ipad as 0x36 repeated for the hash block size, Opad as 0x5c repeated for that size, and Apad as 0x878FE1F3 repeated for one quarter of the hash length.

The sender places Apad in the authentication data field and sets the authentication type to 0x3. It computes an inner hash over the prepared key combined with Ipad and the PDU, then computes an outer hash using the prepared key combined with Opad and the inner result. The outer hash becomes the authentication data.
sections.plainLanguage: HMAC combines the secret key with the PDU in two hash operations. The result is carried in the authentication data field for the receiver to check.

sections.title: Sending and Checking an Authenticated PDU
sections.content:
When sending a PDU, a router selects an active SA. If it cannot find an active key, it discards the PDU. Otherwise it fills the authentication type, length, and Key ID, prepares the fields required by the procedure, computes the HMAC result, and places that result after the Key ID.

When receiving a PDU, the router uses the Key ID to select an SA and recomputes the authentication data. Before computing, it saves the received authentication value, checksum, and remaining lifetime; it substitutes Apad for the authentication value and zero for the other two fields. If the result differs from the received value, it discards the PDU and SHOULD log an error event.

An implementation MAY offer a transition mode that sends CRYPTO_AUTH data without verifying it. The RFC presents this only as an aid for migration.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender calculates an authentication value using its configured key. The receiver repeats the calculation and discards the PDU if the values do not match.

sections.title: Protection Limits and Authentication Type Assignment
sections.content:
CRYPTO_AUTH does not encrypt PDUs and does not protect against replay attacks. An attacker could replay old Hello PDUs to disrupt an adjacency, or replay sequence-number PDUs and cause LSPs to flood the network. The Remaining Lifetime field is not authenticated, so an intermediate system can age an LSP without recomputing its authentication data.

The RFC recommends changing keys periodically and requires implementations to store and use more than one key at a time. It warns that transition mode leaves a router vulnerable and should be limited to migration. IANA registered authentication type 3 for CRYPTO_AUTH in the TLV 10 authentication type registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication can detect a changed message, but this format does not hide messages or stop an old message from being replayed. Transition mode also leaves the router vulnerable because it does not check the authentication value.
